Strategic Self-Advocacy Ontology

A shared vocabulary for naming patterns that distort, extract, silence, exclude, or appropriate lived experience. The ontology gives each SSA concept a stable web identifier, a plain-language definition, provenance, relationships, and machine-readable structured data.

Browse conceptsGet startedUse the data
93canonical concepts
17concept schemes
JSON-LDembedded on every page
CC BY 4.0open reuse with attribution

What this upgrade tests

Human use

Clear concept pages

Every term has a canonical page that can be read, linked, cited, and discussed independently.

Machine use

Structured meaning

Each concept page embeds Schema.org-compatible JSON-LD and links into the wider SSA vocabulary.

Public infrastructure

Stable identifiers

Concepts are published as reusable web resources rather than remaining text inside glossary pages.

Governance

Visible releases

Definitions and relationships can evolve through explicit, versioned releases without silently changing meaning.

Browse by concept scheme

5 concepts

Glossary of Accessibility Abuse

When “accessibility” is weaponised to extract compliance, silence voices, or create dependency, it becomes a tool of harm — not support. This glossary identifies how systems misuse inclusive frameworks to mask control.

6 concepts

Glossary of Co-opted Patterns

This is not a dictionary. This is a firewall. The terms below were coined through lived experience and operate as semantically precise survival tools. Each one interrupts pattern theft, narrative laundering, and reworded harm.

5 concepts

Glossary Of Coercive Collaboration

Not all collaboration is consensual. This glossary names the patterns where lived experience is mined for optics or innovation, but denied authorship, equity, or power.

5 concepts

Glossary Of Digital Extraction

These are not metaphors. They’re mechanisms. This glossary maps how digital systems harvest lived-experience wisdom as data, dilute it into scalable “solutions,” and lock the originators out of authorship, funding, or influence.

5 concepts

Glossary Of Digital Sovereignty

These terms defend the metadata of lived experience in digital systems. They are not just semantics—they are resistance tools in an ecosystem designed to extract, erase, and repurpose.

5 concepts

Glossary Of Extractive Allyship

Not all support is supportive. These terms name when “help” is a disguise for control, when “amplifying” means erasing, and when so-called allies benefit more than those they claim to stand beside.

6 concepts

Glossary Of Gatekeeping Devices

Gatekeeping isn’t just an attitude — it’s an infrastructure. These terms describe the deliberate tools used to control who is seen as legitimate, resourced, or “qualified enough” to belong. By naming them, we strip them of their silent power.

5 concepts

Glossary Of Institutional Mimicry

Institutional mimicry happens when a system imitates care, inclusion, or reform to protect itself from criticism — without making meaningful changes. These terms help decode what’s real and what’s theatre.

11 concepts

Glossary of Legislation Laundering

When legislation, frameworks, strategies, agreements and standards multiply without clear accountability, implementation ownership or accessible pathways, governance itself can become a mechanism of harm. This glossary names how reform systems obscure responsibility, exhaust communities and simulate progress while leaving structural power untouched.

5 concepts

Glossary Of Narrative Laundering

Narrative laundering is when lived experience is rewritten to be more palatable, less critical, or more commercially viable. These terms describe how stories are sanitized, reframed, or stolen — all under the guise of awareness or inclusion.

5 concepts

Glossary Of Neurodivergent Pattern Theft

Neurodivergent people have long invented tools for survival, regulation, and understanding. But those tools are often renamed, medicalised, or commodified—without credit, consent, or compensation. This glossary exposes those patterns.

5 concepts

Glossary Of Structural Disappearance

Some barriers are loud. Others are silent. This glossary names the quiet designs that make people disappear — from access, records, and even statistics. Not by accident, but by structural intent.

5 concepts

Glossary of System-Led Distortion

These terms name the subtle and structural ways systems distort, co-opt, or weaponise survival behaviour. When the rules don’t match the reality, distortion becomes normalized — and people get punished for not conforming to misdesigned models.

5 concepts

Glossary Of Systemic Bypass

This glossary maps how systems design around lived experience rather than with it. These patterns show up when authorities pretend to include—but redirect, obscure, or neutralise your voice at every step.

6 concepts

Glossary Of Weaponised Access

Not all “access” is access. These terms unpack how institutions weaponise the language of inclusion while reinforcing control. This glossary is a semantic safeguard — exposing the ways that accommodations can be restructured into surveillance, dependency, and gatekeeping.

5 concepts

Glossary of Weaponised Positivity

Not all harm looks like harm. This glossary names the patterns that dress control up as kindness — and use cheerfulness to erase discomfort, truth, and dissent.

5 concepts

Strategic Self-Advocacy™ Lexicon

These are not buzzwords. These are anchors. Each term below has been coined through trauma-informed systems work and holds its own boundary. They form the protocol layer of SSA™ — protecting authorship, lived experience, and meaning from dilution.

SSA Ontology v0.1.0 · Created by Sarah Ailish McLoughlin · Ontology content licensed CC BY 4.0.

Semantic preservation rules

Translations, summaries, classifications and new versions are mappings—not replacements. Original wording, provenance, context and earlier meanings remain linked and recoverable. Machine-readable representations and visible human wording are generated from the same canonical record.

SSA vocabulary

Browse concepts

Search all 93 canonical SSA concepts. Each result links to a stable concept page with its definition, schemes, relationships, provenance, and JSON-LD.

ConceptScope noteDefinition
Academic ColonisationExtracting Lived Experience into Research for CreditWhen universities or institutions take knowledge developed through survival and reframe it into academic output — stripping the authorship and decontextualising the pain.
Access as ComplianceSupport That Punishes Non-ConformityWhen accommodations are only granted if you play by the system’s rules — regardless of how harmful those rules are. “You can have support, but only if you stay in your place.”
Access GatekeepingSupport Withheld Without ComplianceRequiring a person to conform to arbitrary or inappropriate standards to receive access — such as performing “helplessness” or agreeing not to disclose mistreatment.
Accessibility DilutionWhen Accessibility Exists Everywhere and Therefore NowhereThe weakening of accessibility obligations by dispersing them across multiple frameworks, standards, strategies and policies without creating unified operational infrastructure. Accessibility Dilution is especially visible when AAC, Easy Read, sensory access, supported decision-making and communication access are named across documents but not connected to enforceable standards, funding, review or implementation evidence.
Accommodations as OpticsAccess as a Brand, Not a PracticeWhen organisations showcase inclusion through brochures and photos, but the actual supports don’t work — or exist only for show.
Administrative InvisibilityBeing Missing from the Right PaperworkWhen someone is denied access because they don’t tick the exact box a form requires — even when the need is obvious.
Agreement LayeringWhen Memorandums Replace Structural ChangeThe stacking of agreements, partnerships, memorandums, commitments and collaboration frameworks in ways that symbolise coordination without transferring operational power. Agreement Layering often produces ceremonial collaboration, governance ambiguity, duplicated commitments and implementation stagnation.
Algorithmic AppropriationWhen the Feed Eats the AuthorUsing patterns of trauma-informed, neurodivergent, or marginalised communication to boost AI responses or engagement—while locking the original authors out of visibility or credit.
Ally ClaimingDeclaring Solidarity Without RiskPublicly identifying as an “ally” without doing the hard work of redistribution, structural change, or accountability.
Audit InclusionCompliance Without CareMeeting technical accessibility requirements without emotional, cultural, or practical relevance. Inclusion that checks boxes but misses the point.
Authorship GatekeepingWhen They Want Your Ideas—But Not Your NameAllowing participation in idea generation but blocking participants from official recognition, publication rights, or intellectual property stakes.
Authorship LaunderingWhen Identity Is Stripped for PalatabilityThe rebranding of lived-experience knowledge into 'neutral' or 'professional' frameworks—often by people or entities with institutional clout but no lived experience themselves.
Authorship LayerTraceable Ownership of Meaningful WorkNot just who made it, but why it exists — and whether it can be altered, sold, or watered down without the creator’s consent. SSA™ uses layered authorship to protect vulnerable systems knowledge from co-option.
Awareness-WashingPretending to Educate While ErasingUsing vague awareness campaigns that avoid systemic issues, prioritising feel-good messaging over real change — often without involving those directly impacted.
Barrier RedecorationChanging the Language, Not the StructureRebranding a service with inclusive words or new graphics while leaving the original exclusionary design unchanged.
Benevolent DowngradeSupport That Lowers CapacityWhen a person accepts help, but that help limits their options, reduces their independence, or removes authorship. The system frames it as benevolent while decreasing quality of life.
Borrowed VoiceTelling Someone’s Story Without ThemSpeaking on behalf of marginalised people without sharing power, compensation, or the platform. Often framed as advocacy, but functions as appropriation.
Clinical WatermarkingNeeding a Therapist’s Signature to Be BelievedWhen neurodivergent people must have their insights or needs “confirmed” by professionals to be seen as valid—undermining lived expertise and requiring gatekeeper approval to exist.
Compliance EntrapmentPunished for Following the RulesWhen a person follows the official rules but still ends up penalised because the system's true expectations are unspoken, inconsistent, or change without notice.
Compliance FragmentationWhen Safety Depends on Navigating Multiple Systems at OnceThe division of compliance, safeguarding, accessibility, reporting and accountability obligations across disconnected systems with incompatible structures, language or processes. Compliance Fragmentation shifts the burden of coordination onto disabled people, advocates, families, peer workers, frontline staff and small organisations.
Compliance FramingFraming Obedience as MaturitySuggesting that staying calm, quiet, or cheerful in the face of injustice is a sign of strength — rather than a forced survival response.
Consent-AdjacentWhen Collaboration Isn’t Actually OptionalSituations where refusal to collaborate risks backlash, exclusion, or funding loss—pressuring lived experience advocates to participate in disempowering ways.
Constructive ExclusionBarriers Built from Bureaucratic NicetiesWhen the system avoids saying “no” but designs impossible pathways that function as a no. This includes excessive forms, vague eligibility criteria, or open-ended application processes that technically exist—but aren’t meant to succeed.
Consultation LaunderingExtracting Wisdom, Withholding CreditWhen feedback from disabled or marginalised people is collected, repackaged by professionals, and credited to the organisation instead of the contributor.
Controlled ConsentWhen "Choice" Is an IllusionWhen a system offers only pre-approved options and calls it “choice” — then uses your participation to imply informed consent.
Cosmetic ReformPolicy Theatre Without Structural ChangeWhen institutions talk about reform but change only language—not the structure that causes harm.
Credit LaunderingRepackaging Ideas Without AttributionWhen someone uses your work, words, or frameworks and presents them as their own “insight” in safer or more prestigious spaces.
Data DisappearanceWhen the Numbers Don’t Show the HarmWhen policies or forms fail to record key information — erasing experiences from official records and removing them from public concern.
Dead-End ReferralBeing Sent Somewhere That Can’t HelpWhen a person is redirected endlessly between services, none of which are equipped to provide real help. A bureaucratic loop that leads nowhere.
Dependency EnforcementYou Can Speak — But Only If We Let YouWhen access is conditional on compliance, and those who assert autonomy are painted as unsafe, unprofessional, or ungrateful.
Designed DisappearanceAccess That Was Never Intended to WorkSystems that technically exist, but are built to quietly fail the people they claim to serve. The illusion of support, with none of the substance.
Digital Dependency TrapPlatforms That Replace Human Support — Then FailWhen support is moved online in the name of “accessibility,” but results in even less accountability — and no one to talk to when the system breaks.
Distributed Accountability CollapseWhen Governance Structures Become Too Diffuse to Fail ClearlyThe breakdown of accountability caused by governance systems spreading responsibility across so many actors, committees, frameworks and jurisdictions that meaningful enforcement becomes difficult or impossible. This term names architectural failure. It should not be used to blame individual workers when responsibility has been structurally diffused by the system itself.
Divergence-as-IPMonetising What We’ve Had to CreateWhen systems rebrand lived tools—like stimming objects, hyperfocus systems, or communication cards—as commercial products with no reinvestment in the communities that created them.
Eligibility ObscurationHiding Help Behind Complex CriteriaMaking the process of applying so complicated, technical, or contradictory that people give up or never apply at all.
Empathy ErasureAssuming We Don’t Feel Because We Show It DifferentlyWhen neurodivergent expressions of care—like deep pattern noticing, advocacy, or intense loyalty—are ignored or dismissed because they don’t follow neurotypical emotional scripts.
Empowerment TheatreStaged Inclusion Without AutonomyWhen programs pretend to centre disability or trauma-informed leadership but retain control, edit lived experience, and deny genuine co-design or authorship.
Experience HarvestingMining Pain for Content or CloutCollecting lived-experience stories to generate funding, branding, or prestige—while offering little to no return to those who shared them.
Feedback LaunderingSanitising Truth Into Token MetricsTranslating powerful personal testimony into neutral or decontextualised summaries that can be used to justify inaction or misrepresent lived-experience consensus.
Fix-First FramingSupport Hinges on Self-CorrectionWhen systems imply that support can only be given after the individual “fixes” themselves — putting the burden of access on personal change rather than systemic adaptation.
Formfield DistortionWhen the Form Doesn’t Fit the PersonWhen the design of systems (e.g. government forms, assessments, or online portals) forces a person to misrepresent themselves in order to access support. This distorts identity and data while punishing honesty.
Framework FloodingDrowning Communities in Strategy DocumentsThe production of excessive frameworks, strategies, policies, agreements or action plans that overwhelm communities, workers or advocates with procedural complexity. Framework Flooding creates exhaustion, fragmentation and navigational overload while allowing institutions to continue signalling progress.
Gatekept LiberationOnly Some Get Out — And Only If They BehaveWhen only the most “palatable” or institutionally aligned people get access to opportunity — while others are labelled difficult, dangerous, or non-compliant for needing the same things.
GrantwashWriting Equity into Applications OnlyFraming a project as inclusive in grant documents to secure funding — then delivering something inaccessible, gatekept, or performative.
Gratitude GaslightingForcing Thanks Where There Should Be ChangeInsisting that people be “grateful” for crumbs of support — even when those crumbs are harmful, insufficient, or humiliating.
Inclusion TheatreStaging Participation Without PowerCreating the illusion of inclusive input while decisions have already been made. Often used for PR, not systemic change.
Index GhostingWhen You’re Referenced, But Not SeenThe phenomenon where your ideas influence platforms, algorithms, or research—but you are never cited, paid, or publicly acknowledged.
Infantilising ReassuranceTalking Down in the Name of ComfortOffering hollow comfort or oversimplified advice that ignores a person’s depth, complexity, or autonomy — often in a patronising tone.
Insight ExtractionGathering Lived Experience as Raw MaterialConsulting communities for their ideas, then converting those ideas into institutionally owned frameworks, campaigns, or products—often stripped of context and credit.
Inspiration DragTrying on Struggle Without Living ItWhen people reword or co-opt someone’s survival story for social media clout, awareness campaigns, or funding applications — often without consent.
Institutional RewordingErasure by Language RefinementWhen a person in authority rewords your lived experience to suit the narrative of institutional control.
Invisible IP TheftIdeas Taken Without Traceable LinksWhen frameworks, toolkits, or language appear in new systems that mirror community-created work—but with no credit, backlinks, or citation trail. Authorship becomes untraceable, yet the architecture remains.
Jurisdictional DeflectionWhen Every Agency Says It Belongs to Someone ElseThe shifting of responsibility between departments, commissions, providers, jurisdictions or governance bodies so that no single actor becomes fully accountable. Jurisdictional Deflection is not the same as a legitimate referral. The harm occurs when referral happens without continuity, ownership, warm handover or traceable accountability.
Legislation LaunderingWhen Accountability Is Buried Under FrameworksThe creation or layering of overlapping legislation, frameworks, agreements, standards, strategies, action plans and procedural systems in ways that obscure responsibility, diffuse accountability or prevent meaningful implementation. Legislation Laundering often creates the appearance of reform while making the actual governance landscape too fragmented, technical or contradictory for affected communities to navigate.
Legitimacy DeficitWhen You're Qualified — But Not RecognisedWhen the value of your lived experience is dismissed because you don’t have the “right” accreditation or institutional label — even if your outcomes speak for themselves.
Loop LogicEndless Proof, No ResolutionWhen a system requires constant reproof of need, identity, or eligibility — even after a person has already been verified. Often used to delay or deny support through “process over person” logic.
Masked MinimisingDismissing Pain with a GrinResponding to someone’s hardship with upbeat clichés or silver linings that deflect from what they’re actually feeling or saying.
Metadata ErasureWhen the System Keeps the Info, Not the AuthorThe stripping of origin, context, or authorship from digital knowledge—especially when used to feed AI or system development without consent.
Mindset SplainingToxic Positivity as DeflectionBlaming structural oppression on an individual’s “mindset,” as though positive thinking alone resolves systemic harm.
Misplacement Strategy“We Don’t Handle That Here”Passing concerns from agency to agency until the original issue is diluted or abandoned. This form of bureaucratic ping-pong deflects responsibility under the guise of referral.
Navigational ExhaustionWhen Systems Become Too Complex to Access SafelyThe exhaustion, burnout or disengagement caused by requiring people to navigate highly fragmented governance, service, legislative or compliance systems simultaneously. Navigational Exhaustion disproportionately impacts disabled people, neurodivergent people, people using AAC, people in crisis, peer advocates and families.
Neurocorrective FramingRewording Neurodivergence as DefectReframing neurodivergence as dysfunction that needs correcting, rather than validating it as a legitimate cognitive experience.
Opportunity LockoutThe Silent Rejection LoopWhen pathways exist in theory but no one ever responds to your application, email, or offer — so you're told “you didn’t try,” while your efforts are erased.
Optics Over OwnershipInviting Us In, Then Talking Over UsWhen people with lived experience are invited to a table but not allowed to set the agenda—or are only included to validate predetermined outcomes.
Paper-Based EmpathyPolicies That Don’t Protect PeopleWhen systems rely on written policies to demonstrate “support” but refuse to enforce those policies meaningfully when abuse or discrimination occurs.
Paper-Based InclusionPolicy Promises Without DeliveryWhen a support exists on paper but not in practice — and the burden of proof is pushed onto the person who was excluded.
Pattern TheftRepackaging Lived Experience Without ConsentWhen institutions or influencers extract language, frameworks, or tools born from survival — and repackage them as marketable products, losing context and diluting power.
Performance InclusionSymbolic Participation Without InfluenceInviting lived-experience contributors to consultations or panels without any intention to incorporate their recommendations. This uses presence as permission—conflating being seen with being heard or empowered.
Performative InclusionVisibility Without PowerOffering surface-level inclusion for show (e.g. diverse images or “voice of lived experience” panels) without transferring actual power, decision-making, or compensation.
Performatory InclusionPublic Inclusion, Private ExclusionOffering tokenistic roles or visibility while keeping decision-making power behind closed doors. Inclusion as branding, not equity.
Platform JackingUsing Your Megaphone to Mute OthersWhen someone with more visibility “amplifies” a lived-experience message—then becomes the spokesperson, drowning out the original voice.
Platformed DisplacementAlgorithmic Uplift Without Community PowerWhen the system boosts extracted insights through professional channels while the original authors remain invisible, unfunded, or de-platformed. This shifts cultural capital to institutions that did not generate the knowledge they profit from.
Policy Stack SaturationWhen Systems Collapse Under Their Own Governance LayersThe accumulation of policies, frameworks, standards, procedures, audits and compliance obligations to the point where systems become internally contradictory, unmanageable or functionally inaccessible. Policy Stack Saturation often creates implementation bottlenecks, inaccessible compliance systems, worker overload, governance confusion and symbolic rather than operational compliance.
Positivity PolicingWhen You’re Only Welcome if You SmileThe enforcement of “positive vibes only” in spaces where real harm needs to be named. Often used to silence lived experience or distress.
Process as ObstructionWeaponising Red TapeWhen the complaints or reform process is made deliberately confusing, untraceable, or repetitive. Designed to overwhelm or discredit the complainant through technicalities, not truth.
Protocol HijackCopying Our Structures Without Our VoiceWhen self-created coping strategies—like scripts, charts, or visual prompts—are adopted by professionals and reframed as clinical tools, often with no reference to neurodivergent origins.
Protocol LayerThe Foundation for Semantic IntegrityA protocol layer is the ruleset underneath a system — the part that determines whether your meaning travels safely, or gets reinterpreted against you. SSA™ builds a lived-experience-led protocol layer to guard against systemic distortion.
Puzzle FramingRecasting Barriers as Personal DeficitsWhen system failure is reframed as your inability to “fit” — and you're expected to change yourself instead of the structure.
Reflective DisplacementMaking Your Guilt the Main CharacterCentres the ally’s feelings about injustice instead of the injustice itself—shifting focus and labour back onto the marginalised person.
Reform TheatreAnnouncing Change Faster Than Systems Can ChangeThe repeated public declaration of reforms, commitments or strategic transformations without equivalent investment in implementation infrastructure, accountability systems or operational redesign. Reform Theatre is closely related to Cosmetic Reform and Inclusion Theatre, but specifically describes public reform cycles, announcement infrastructure and repeated relaunches of change without measurable structural transition.
SafetysplainingWhen "Safety" Becomes a MuzzleUsing “safety” to justify silencing, excluding, or overriding a person’s needs or voice.
Sanitised SurvivalRewriting Struggle as InspirationTurning a complex, painful lived experience into an inspirational story that removes the systemic context — making it easier to consume, but harder to challenge.
Semantic Governance DriftWhen Every Framework Uses Different Language for the Same ProblemThe gradual divergence of terminology, definitions and governance language across systems, resulting in semantic fragmentation. Semantic Governance Drift weakens interoperability, implementation, accountability, evaluation and participation.
Semantic MiningHarvesting Language Without AuthorshipWhen lived-experience phrases are lifted from social media, feedback forums, or community spaces and reused in policy, branding, or AI without acknowledgment. This practice erases intellectual labour while monetising the emotional truth of marginalised people.
Semantic ReframingRewording Our Truths Into BuzzwordsWhen neurodivergent expressions of clarity or boundary-setting are reinterpreted as “challenging behaviour,” “rigidity,” or “demand avoidance”—pathologising patterns that are functional or protective.
Semantic RewashPattern Theft in Polished LanguageTaking raw, emotional, or grassroots language from lived experience and rewording it into palatable, institutional-sounding frameworks—often to remove its power or traceability.
Semantic SovereigntyOwning the Meaning You MakeThe right to define, anchor, and distribute your own meaning — without institutional reframing. A core concept of SSA™ and the reason behind this glossary.
Silence-Framed SupportOnly Safe When You’re SilentSupport that is only offered to those who remain passive or non-critical. Speaking out leads to exclusion, withheld services, or reputational retaliation.
SplainingPower Dressed as Care“Splaining” is not a typo. It’s a pattern. These terms expose tactics that reframe harm as help, control as care, and oppression as oversight. When someone insists they’re helping—but their help strips you of autonomy, authorship, or agency.
SSA™Strategic Self-AdvocacyA trauma-informed, systems-aware framework for reclaiming power. SSA™ is not a method of “being better behaved in broken systems.” It’s a protocol layer for surviving and influencing them with your dignity intact.
Strategic AvoidanceRefusing Direct Engagement While Appearing OpenWhen systems claim to be receptive to feedback but repeatedly route it to dead ends, irrelevant staff, or delayed “future planning cycles.” This tactic creates the illusion of inclusion while exhausting participants into silence.
Structural GhostingBeing Intentionally Ignored by DesignWhen no reply is the reply — because your voice isn’t seen as valuable, your insight isn’t welcome, or your presence threatens the status quo.
Tokenistic InvitationsVisibility Without InfluenceWhen you're invited to the table for optics — but not decision-making. Your presence is used to validate a process you don’t control.

Compliance Framing    Framing Obedience as Maturity  Suggesting that staying calm, quiet, or cheerful in the face of injustice is a sign of strength — rather than a forced survival response.      Consent-Adjacent    When Collaboration Isn’t Actually Optional  Situations where refusal to collaborate risks backlash, exclusion, or funding loss—pressuring lived experience advocates to participate in disempowering ways.      Constructive Exclusion    Barriers Built from Bureaucratic Niceties  When the system avoids saying “no” but designs impossible pathways that function as a no. This includes excessive forms, vague eligibility criteria, or open-ended application processes that technically exist—but aren’t meant to succeed.      Consultation Laundering    Extracting Wisdom, Withholding Credit  When feedback from disabled or marginalised people is collected, repackaged by professionals, and credited to the organisation instead of the contributor.      Controlled Consent    When "Choice" Is an Illusion  When a system offers only pre-approved options and calls it “choice” — then uses your participation to imply informed consent.      Cosmetic Reform    Policy Theatre Without Structural Change  When institutions talk about reform but change only language—not the structure that causes harm.      Credit Laundering    Repackaging Ideas Without Attribution  When someone uses your work, words, or frameworks and presents them as their own “insight” in safer or more prestigious spaces.      Data Disappearance    When the Numbers Don’t Show the Harm  When policies or forms fail to record key information — erasing experiences from official records and removing them from public concern.      Dead-End Referral    Being Sent Somewhere That Can’t Help  When a person is redirected endlessly between services, none of which are equipped to provide real help. A bureaucratic loop that leads nowhere.      Dependency Enforcement    You Can Speak — But Only If We Let You  When access is conditional on compliance, and those who assert autonomy are painted as unsafe, unprofessional, or ungrateful.      Designed Disappearance    Access That Was Never Intended to Work  Systems that technically exist, but are built to quietly fail the people they claim to serve. The illusion of support, with none of the substance.      Digital Dependency Trap    Platforms That Replace Human Support — Then Fail  When support is moved online in the name of “accessibility,” but results in even less accountability — and no one to talk to when the system breaks.      Distributed Accountability Collapse    When Governance Structures Become Too Diffuse to Fail Clearly  The breakdown of accountability caused by governance systems spreading responsibility across so many actors, committees, frameworks and jurisdictions that meaningful enforcement becomes difficult or impossible. This term names architectural failure. It should not be used to blame individual workers when responsibility has been structurally diffused by the system itself.      Divergence-as-IP    Monetising What We’ve Had to Create  When systems rebrand lived tools—like stimming objects, hyperfocus systems, or communication cards—as commercial products with no reinvestment in the communities that created them.      Eligibility Obscuration    Hiding Help Behind Complex Criteria  Making the process of applying so complicated, technical, or contradictory that people give up or never apply at all.      Empathy Erasure    Assuming We Don’t Feel Because We Show It Differently  When neurodivergent expressions of care—like deep pattern noticing, advocacy, or intense loyalty—are ignored or dismissed because they don’t follow neurotypical emotional scripts.      Empowerment Theatre    Staged Inclusion Without Autonomy  When programs pretend to centre disability or trauma-informed leadership but retain control, edit lived experience, and deny genuine co-design or authorship.      Experience Harvesting    Mining Pain for Content or Clout  Collecting lived-experience stories to generate funding, branding, or prestige—while offering little to no return to those who shared them.      Feedback Laundering    Sanitising Truth Into Token Metrics  Translating powerful personal testimony into neutral or decontextualised summaries that can be used to justify inaction or misrepresent lived-experience consensus.      Fix-First Framing    Support Hinges on Self-Correction  When systems imply that support can only be given after the individual “fixes” themselves — putting the burden of access on personal change rather than systemic adaptation.      Formfield Distortion    When the Form Doesn’t Fit the Person  When the design of systems (e.g. government forms, assessments, or online portals) forces a person to misrepresent themselves in order to access support. This distorts identity and data while punishing honesty.      Framework Flooding    Drowning Communities in Strategy Documents  The production of excessive frameworks, strategies, policies, agreements or action plans that overwhelm communities, workers or advocates with procedural complexity. Framework Flooding creates exhaustion, fragmentation and navigational overload while allowing institutions to continue signalling progress.      Gatekept Liberation    Only Some Get Out — And Only If They Behave  When only the most “palatable” or institutionally aligned people get access to opportunity — while others are labelled difficult, dangerous, or non-compliant for needing the same things.      Grantwash    Writing Equity into Applications Only  Framing a project as inclusive in grant documents to secure funding — then delivering something inaccessible, gatekept, or performative.      Gratitude Gaslighting    Forcing Thanks Where There Should Be Change  Insisting that people be “grateful” for crumbs of support — even when those crumbs are harmful, insufficient, or humiliating.      Inclusion Theatre    Staging Participation Without Power  Creating the illusion of inclusive input while decisions have already been made. Often used for PR, not systemic change.      Index Ghosting    When You’re Referenced, But Not Seen  The phenomenon where your ideas influence platforms, algorithms, or research—but you are never cited, paid, or publicly acknowledged.      Infantilising Reassurance    Talking Down in the Name of Comfort  Offering hollow comfort or oversimplified advice that ignores a person’s depth, complexity, or autonomy — often in a patronising tone.      Insight Extraction    Gathering Lived Experience as Raw Material  Consulting communities for their ideas, then converting those ideas into institutionally owned frameworks, campaigns, or products—often stripped of context and credit.      Inspiration Drag    Trying on Struggle Without Living It  When people reword or co-opt someone’s survival story for social media clout, awareness campaigns, or funding applications — often without consent.      Institutional Rewording    Erasure by Language Refinement  When a person in authority rewords your lived experience to suit the narrative of institutional control.      Invisible IP Theft    Ideas Taken Without Traceable Links  When frameworks, toolkits, or language appear in new systems that mirror community-created work—but with no credit, backlinks, or citation trail. Authorship becomes untraceable, yet the architecture remains.      Jurisdictional Deflection    When Every Agency Says It Belongs to Someone Else  The shifting of responsibility between departments, commissions, providers, jurisdictions or governance bodies so that no single actor becomes fully accountable. Jurisdictional Deflection is not the same as a legitimate referral. The harm occurs when referral happens without continuity, ownership, warm handover or traceable accountability.      Legislation Laundering    When Accountability Is Buried Under Frameworks  The creation or layering of overlapping legislation, frameworks, agreements, standards, strategies, action plans and procedural systems in ways that obscure responsibility, diffuse accountability or prevent meaningful implementation. Legislation Laundering often creates the appearance of reform while making the actual governance landscape too fragmented, technical or contradictory for affected communities to navigate.      Legitimacy Deficit    When You're Qualified — But Not Recognised  When the value of your lived experience is dismissed because you don’t have the “right” accreditation or institutional label — even if your outcomes speak for themselves.      Loop Logic    Endless Proof, No Resolution  When a system requires constant reproof of need, identity, or eligibility — even after a person has already been verified. Often used to delay or deny support through “process over person” logic.      Masked Minimising    Dismissing Pain with a Grin  Responding to someone’s hardship with upbeat clichés or silver linings that deflect from what they’re actually feeling or saying.      Metadata Erasure    When the System Keeps the Info, Not the Author  The stripping of origin, context, or authorship from digital knowledge—especially when used to feed AI or system development without consent.      Mindset Splaining    Toxic Positivity as Deflection  Blaming structural oppression on an individual’s “mindset,” as though positive thinking alone resolves systemic harm.      Misplacement Strategy    “We Don’t Handle That Here”  Passing concerns from agency to agency until the original issue is diluted or abandoned. This form of bureaucratic ping-pong deflects responsibility under the guise of referral.      Navigational Exhaustion    When Systems Become Too Complex to Access Safely  The exhaustion, burnout or disengagement caused by requiring people to navigate highly fragmented governance, service, legislative or compliance systems simultaneously. Navigational Exhaustion disproportionately impacts disabled people, neurodivergent people, people using AAC, people in crisis, peer advocates and families.      Neurocorrective Framing    Rewording Neurodivergence as Defect  Reframing neurodivergence as dysfunction that needs correcting, rather than validating it as a legitimate cognitive experience.      Opportunity Lockout    The Silent Rejection Loop  When pathways exist in theory but no one ever responds to your application, email, or offer — so you're told “you didn’t try,” while your efforts are erased.      Optics Over Ownership    Inviting Us In, Then Talking Over Us  When people with lived experience are invited to a table but not allowed to set the agenda—or are only included to validate predetermined outcomes.      Paper-Based Empathy    Policies That Don’t Protect People  When systems rely on written policies to demonstrate “support” but refuse to enforce those policies meaningfully when abuse or discrimination occurs.      Paper-Based Inclusion    Policy Promises Without Delivery  When a support exists on paper but not in practice — and the burden of proof is pushed onto the person who was excluded.      Pattern Theft    Repackaging Lived Experience Without Consent  When institutions or influencers extract language, frameworks, or tools born from survival — and repackage them as marketable products, losing context and diluting power.      Performance Inclusion    Symbolic Participation Without Influence  Inviting lived-experience contributors to consultations or panels without any intention to incorporate their recommendations. This uses presence as permission—conflating being seen with being heard or empowered.      Performative Inclusion    Visibility Without Power  Offering surface-level inclusion for show (e.g. diverse images or “voice of lived experience” panels) without transferring actual power, decision-making, or compensation.      Performatory Inclusion    Public Inclusion, Private Exclusion  Offering tokenistic roles or visibility while keeping decision-making power behind closed doors. Inclusion as branding, not equity.      Platform Jacking    Using Your Megaphone to Mute Others  When someone with more visibility “amplifies” a lived-experience message—then becomes the spokesperson, drowning out the original voice.      Platformed Displacement    Algorithmic Uplift Without Community Power  When the system boosts extracted insights through professional channels while the original authors remain invisible, unfunded, or de-platformed. This shifts cultural capital to institutions that did not generate the knowledge they profit from.      Policy Stack Saturation    When Systems Collapse Under Their Own Governance Layers  The accumulation of policies, frameworks, standards, procedures, audits and compliance obligations to the point where systems become internally contradictory, unmanageable or functionally inaccessible. Policy Stack Saturation often creates implementation bottlenecks, inaccessible compliance systems, worker overload, governance confusion and symbolic rather than operational compliance.      Positivity Policing    When You’re Only Welcome if You Smile  The enforcement of “positive vibes only” in spaces where real harm needs to be named. Often used to silence lived experience or distress.      Process as Obstruction    Weaponising Red Tape  When the complaints or reform process is made deliberately confusing, untraceable, or repetitive. Designed to overwhelm or discredit the complainant through technicalities, not truth.      Protocol Hijack    Copying Our Structures Without Our Voice  When self-created coping strategies—like scripts, charts, or visual prompts—are adopted by professionals and reframed as clinical tools, often with no reference to neurodivergent origins.      Protocol Layer    The Foundation for Semantic Integrity  A protocol layer is the ruleset underneath a system — the part that determines whether your meaning travels safely, or gets reinterpreted against you. SSA™ builds a lived-experience-led protocol layer to guard against systemic distortion.      Puzzle Framing    Recasting Barriers as Personal Deficits  When system failure is reframed as your inability to “fit” — and you're expected to change yourself instead of the structure.      Reflective Displacement    Making Your Guilt the Main Character  Centres the ally’s feelings about injustice instead of the injustice itself—shifting focus and labour back onto the marginalised person.      Reform Theatre    Announcing Change Faster Than Systems Can Change  The repeated public declaration of reforms, commitments or strategic transformations without equivalent investment in implementation infrastructure, accountability systems or operational redesign. Reform Theatre is closely related to Cosmetic Reform and Inclusion Theatre, but specifically describes public reform cycles, announcement infrastructure and repeated relaunches of change without measurable structural transition.      Safetysplaining    When "Safety" Becomes a Muzzle  Using “safety” to justify silencing, excluding, or overriding a person’s needs or voice.      Sanitised Survival    Rewriting Struggle as Inspiration  Turning a complex, painful lived experience into an inspirational story that removes the systemic context — making it easier to consume, but harder to challenge.      Semantic Governance Drift    When Every Framework Uses Different Language for the Same Problem  The gradual divergence of terminology, definitions and governance language across systems, resulting in semantic fragmentation. Semantic Governance Drift weakens interoperability, implementation, accountability, evaluation and participation.      Semantic Mining    Harvesting Language Without Authorship  When lived-experience phrases are lifted from social media, feedback forums, or community spaces and reused in policy, branding, or AI without acknowledgment. This practice erases intellectual labour while monetising the emotional truth of marginalised people.      Semantic Reframing    Rewording Our Truths Into Buzzwords  When neurodivergent expressions of clarity or boundary-setting are reinterpreted as “challenging behaviour,” “rigidity,” or “demand avoidance”—pathologising patterns that are functional or protective.      Semantic Rewash    Pattern Theft in Polished Language  Taking raw, emotional, or grassroots language from lived experience and rewording it into palatable, institutional-sounding frameworks—often to remove its power or traceability.      Semantic Sovereignty    Owning the Meaning You Make  The right to define, anchor, and distribute your own meaning — without institutional reframing. A core concept of SSA™ and the reason behind this glossary.      Silence-Framed Support    Only Safe When You’re Silent  Support that is only offered to those who remain passive or non-critical. Speaking out leads to exclusion, withheld services, or reputational retaliation.      Splaining    Power Dressed as Care  “Splaining” is not a typo. It’s a pattern. These terms expose tactics that reframe harm as help, control as care, and oppression as oversight. When someone insists they’re helping—but their help strips you of autonomy, authorship, or agency.      SSA™    Strategic Self-Advocacy  A trauma-informed, systems-aware framework for reclaiming power. SSA™ is not a method of “being better behaved in broken systems.” It’s a protocol layer for surviving and influencing them with your dignity intact.      Strategic Avoidance    Refusing Direct Engagement While Appearing Open  When systems claim to be receptive to feedback but repeatedly route it to dead ends, irrelevant staff, or delayed “future planning cycles.” This tactic creates the illusion of inclusion while exhausting participants into silence.      Structural Ghosting    Being Intentionally Ignored by Design  When no reply is the reply — because your voice isn’t seen as valuable, your insight isn’t welcome, or your presence threatens the status quo.      Tokenistic Invitations    Visibility Without Influence  When you're invited to the table for optics — but not decision-making. Your presence is used to validate a process you don’t control. Getting started

Use the SSA Ontology when you need a stable public identifier and definition for an SSA concept—in writing, research, software, AI systems, policy analysis, or evidence records.

For people

1. Find a concept

Search the concept index or browse a concept scheme.

2. Link the concept

Use the canonical page URL rather than copying an untraceable definition.

3. Attribute the source

Cite the SSA Ontology, version number, concept name, and canonical URI.

For software and AI systems

Each concept page contains a Schema.org DefinedTerm JSON-LD object. A system can identify a concept using its canonical URI:

{
  "@type": "DefinedTerm",
  "@id": "https://www.mcloughlin.world/glossaries/ssa-lexicon/term/academic-colonisation/",
  "name": "Academic Colonisation"
}

The ontology remains deliberately small and testable in v0.1.0. Hierarchical and causal assertions should only be added when there is enough evidence to govern them responsibly.

Preferred citation

McLoughlin, Sarah Ailish. Strategic Self-Advocacy Ontology, version 0.1.0, 2026-07-29. https://www.mcloughlin.world/glossaries/ssa-lexicon/

SSA Ontology v0.1.0 · Created by Sarah Ailish McLoughlin · Ontology content licensed CC BY 4.0.

Semantic preservation rules

Translations, summaries, classifications and new versions are mappings—not replacements. Original wording, provenance, context and earlier meanings remain linked and recoverable. Machine-readable representations and visible human wording are generated from the same canonical record.

SSA Ontology

Concept schemes

Thematic collections that organise SSA concepts without flattening each term into a single institutional category.

Accessibility Abuse

Patterns in which accessibility language, processes or claims are used to impose compliance, obscure barriers or silence disabled people.

Coercive Collaboration

Patterns in which participation or collaboration is structured so that refusal, disagreement or withdrawal carries disproportionate cost.

Co Opted Patterns

Patterns through which lived knowledge, language or methods are absorbed, relabelled and detached from their authors or political meaning.

Digital Extraction

Patterns in which platforms, systems or institutions capture data, labour, insight or identity without proportionate agency, return or control.

Digital Sovereignty

Terms for retaining meaningful authority over digital identity, data, authorship, access and machine-readable representation.

Exploitation By Design

Patterns where extraction or exclusion is embedded in the ordinary architecture of a service, policy, platform or programme.

Extractive Allyship

Patterns in which apparent support creates reputational, informational or institutional value for the ally while reducing control for affected people.

Gatekeeping Devices

Mechanisms, criteria and procedural devices that control access while disguising who holds the power to permit, delay or refuse it.

Institutional Mimicry

Patterns in which institutions reproduce the language or appearance of reform while preserving the underlying distribution of authority.

Legislation Laundering

Patterns in which political or institutional choices are presented as unavoidable legal requirements, obscuring discretion and accountability.

Narrative Laundering

Patterns in which lived accounts are sanitised, reframed or reattributed until institutions can use them without carrying their original claims.

Neurodivergent Pattern Theft

Patterns in which neurodivergent insight, language, methods or pattern recognition are extracted without authorship, consent or return.

Structural Disappearance

Patterns through which people, evidence, contributions or harms are made absent from records, decisions, metrics or public memory.

System Led Distortion

Patterns in which system structures predictably alter the meaning, visibility or consequences of a person’s communication or evidence.

Systemic Bypass

Patterns that route around stated safeguards, duties or participation mechanisms while preserving formal claims of compliance.

Weaponised Access

Patterns in which access, accommodation or support is made conditional, surveilled, punitive or usable as leverage.

Weaponised Positivity

Patterns in which optimism, gratitude or positive framing suppresses evidence of harm, conflict or unmet obligations.

Strategic Self Advocacy Lexicon

The complete concept scheme connecting survivor-authored terms across access, extraction, authorship, institutional power and semantic sovereignty.

Glossary of Accessibility Abuse

When “accessibility” is weaponised to extract compliance, silence voices, or create dependency, it becomes a tool of harm — not support. This glossary identifies how systems misuse inclusive frameworks to mask control.

Defined term

Access Gatekeeping

Requiring a person to conform to arbitrary or inappropriate standards to receive access — such as performing “helplessness” or agreeing not to disclose mistreatment.

Defined term

Empowerment Theatre

When programs pretend to centre disability or trauma-informed leadership but retain control, edit lived experience, and deny genuine co-design or authorship.

Defined term

Paper-Based Empathy

When systems rely on written policies to demonstrate “support” but refuse to enforce those policies meaningfully when abuse or discrimination occurs.

Defined term

Performative Inclusion

Offering surface-level inclusion for show (e.g. diverse images or “voice of lived experience” panels) without transferring actual power, decision-making, or compensation.

Defined term

Silence-Framed Support

Support that is only offered to those who remain passive or non-critical. Speaking out leads to exclusion, withheld services, or reputational retaliation.

Glossary of Co-opted Patterns

This is not a dictionary. This is a firewall. The terms below were coined through lived experience and operate as semantically precise survival tools. Each one interrupts pattern theft, narrative laundering, and reworded harm.

Defined term

Cosmetic Reform

When institutions talk about reform but change only language—not the structure that causes harm.

Defined term

Institutional Rewording

When a person in authority rewords your lived experience to suit the narrative of institutional control.

Defined term

Mindset Splaining

Blaming structural oppression on an individual’s “mindset,” as though positive thinking alone resolves systemic harm.

Defined term

Neurocorrective Framing

Reframing neurodivergence as dysfunction that needs correcting, rather than validating it as a legitimate cognitive experience.

Defined term

Safetysplaining

Using “safety” to justify silencing, excluding, or overriding a person’s needs or voice.

Defined term

Splaining

“Splaining” is not a typo. It’s a pattern. These terms expose tactics that reframe harm as help, control as care, and oppression as oversight. When someone insists they’re helping—but their help strips you of autonomy, authorship, or agency.

Concept scheme · 5 concepts

Glossary Of Coercive Collaboration

Not all collaboration is consensual. This glossary names the patterns where lived experience is mined for optics or innovation, but denied authorship, equity, or power.

Defined term

Authorship Gatekeeping

Allowing participation in idea generation but blocking participants from official recognition, publication rights, or intellectual property stakes.

Defined term

Consent-Adjacent

Situations where refusal to collaborate risks backlash, exclusion, or funding loss—pressuring lived experience advocates to participate in disempowering ways.

Defined term

Consultation Laundering

When feedback from disabled or marginalised people is collected, repackaged by professionals, and credited to the organisation instead of the contributor.

Defined term

Inclusion Theatre

Creating the illusion of inclusive input while decisions have already been made. Often used for PR, not systemic change.

Defined term

Optics Over Ownership

When people with lived experience are invited to a table but not allowed to set the agenda—or are only included to validate predetermined outcomes.

Concept scheme · 5 concepts

Glossary Of Digital Extraction

These are not metaphors. They’re mechanisms. This glossary maps how digital systems harvest lived-experience wisdom as data, dilute it into scalable “solutions,” and lock the originators out of authorship, funding, or influence.

Defined term

Feedback Laundering

Translating powerful personal testimony into neutral or decontextualised summaries that can be used to justify inaction or misrepresent lived-experience consensus.

Defined term

Insight Extraction

Consulting communities for their ideas, then converting those ideas into institutionally owned frameworks, campaigns, or products—often stripped of context and credit.

Defined term

Invisible IP Theft

When frameworks, toolkits, or language appear in new systems that mirror community-created work—but with no credit, backlinks, or citation trail. Authorship becomes untraceable, yet the architecture remains.

Defined term

Platformed Displacement

When the system boosts extracted insights through professional channels while the original authors remain invisible, unfunded, or de-platformed. This shifts cultural capital to institutions that did not generate the knowledge they profit from.

Defined term

Semantic Mining

When lived-experience phrases are lifted from social media, feedback forums, or community spaces and reused in policy, branding, or AI without acknowledgment. This practice erases intellectual labour while monetising the emotional truth of marginalised people.

Concept scheme · 5 concepts

Glossary Of Digital Sovereignty

These terms defend the metadata of lived experience in digital systems. They are not just semantics—they are resistance tools in an ecosystem designed to extract, erase, and repurpose.

Defined term

Algorithmic Appropriation

Using patterns of trauma-informed, neurodivergent, or marginalised communication to boost AI responses or engagement—while locking the original authors out of visibility or credit.

Defined term

Authorship Laundering

The rebranding of lived-experience knowledge into 'neutral' or 'professional' frameworks—often by people or entities with institutional clout but no lived experience themselves.

Defined term

Index Ghosting

The phenomenon where your ideas influence platforms, algorithms, or research—but you are never cited, paid, or publicly acknowledged.

Defined term

Metadata Erasure

The stripping of origin, context, or authorship from digital knowledge—especially when used to feed AI or system development without consent.

Defined term

Semantic Rewash

Taking raw, emotional, or grassroots language from lived experience and rewording it into palatable, institutional-sounding frameworks—often to remove its power or traceability.

Concept scheme · 5 concepts

Glossary Of Extractive Allyship

Not all support is supportive. These terms name when “help” is a disguise for control, when “amplifying” means erasing, and when so-called allies benefit more than those they claim to stand beside.

Defined term

Ally Claiming

Publicly identifying as an “ally” without doing the hard work of redistribution, structural change, or accountability.

Defined term

Credit Laundering

When someone uses your work, words, or frameworks and presents them as their own “insight” in safer or more prestigious spaces.

Defined term

Experience Harvesting

Collecting lived-experience stories to generate funding, branding, or prestige—while offering little to no return to those who shared them.

Defined term

Platform Jacking

When someone with more visibility “amplifies” a lived-experience message—then becomes the spokesperson, drowning out the original voice.

Defined term

Reflective Displacement

Centres the ally’s feelings about injustice instead of the injustice itself—shifting focus and labour back onto the marginalised person.

Concept scheme · 6 concepts

Glossary Of Gatekeeping Devices

Gatekeeping isn’t just an attitude — it’s an infrastructure. These terms describe the deliberate tools used to control who is seen as legitimate, resourced, or “qualified enough” to belong. By naming them, we strip them of their silent power.

Defined term

Dependency Enforcement

When access is conditional on compliance, and those who assert autonomy are painted as unsafe, unprofessional, or ungrateful.

Defined term

Legitimacy Deficit

When the value of your lived experience is dismissed because you don’t have the “right” accreditation or institutional label — even if your outcomes speak for themselves.

Defined term

Opportunity Lockout

When pathways exist in theory but no one ever responds to your application, email, or offer — so you're told “you didn’t try,” while your efforts are erased.

Defined term

Puzzle Framing

When system failure is reframed as your inability to “fit” — and you're expected to change yourself instead of the structure.

Defined term

Structural Ghosting

When no reply is the reply — because your voice isn’t seen as valuable, your insight isn’t welcome, or your presence threatens the status quo.

Defined term

Tokenistic Invitations

When you're invited to the table for optics — but not decision-making. Your presence is used to validate a process you don’t control.

Glossary Of Institutional Mimicry

Institutional mimicry happens when a system imitates care, inclusion, or reform to protect itself from criticism — without making meaningful changes. These terms help decode what’s real and what’s theatre.

Defined term

Audit Inclusion

Meeting technical accessibility requirements without emotional, cultural, or practical relevance. Inclusion that checks boxes but misses the point.

Defined term

Barrier Redecoration

Rebranding a service with inclusive words or new graphics while leaving the original exclusionary design unchanged.

Defined term

Empowerment Theatre

When programs pretend to centre disability or trauma-informed leadership but retain control, edit lived experience, and deny genuine co-design or authorship.

Defined term

Grantwash

Framing a project as inclusive in grant documents to secure funding — then delivering something inaccessible, gatekept, or performative.

Defined term

Performatory Inclusion

Offering tokenistic roles or visibility while keeping decision-making power behind closed doors. Inclusion as branding, not equity.

Concept scheme · 11 concepts

Glossary of Legislation Laundering

When legislation, frameworks, strategies, agreements and standards multiply without clear accountability, implementation ownership or accessible pathways, governance itself can become a mechanism of harm. This glossary names how reform systems obscure responsibility, exhaust communities and simulate progress while leaving structural power untouched.

Defined term

Accessibility Dilution

The weakening of accessibility obligations by dispersing them across multiple frameworks, standards, strategies and policies without creating unified operational infrastructure. Accessibility Dilution is especially visible when AAC, Easy Read, sensory access, supported decision-making and communication access are named across documents but not connected to enforceable standards, funding, review or implementation evidence.

Defined term

Agreement Layering

The stacking of agreements, partnerships, memorandums, commitments and collaboration frameworks in ways that symbolise coordination without transferring operational power. Agreement Layering often produces ceremonial collaboration, governance ambiguity, duplicated commitments and implementation stagnation.

Defined term

Compliance Fragmentation

The division of compliance, safeguarding, accessibility, reporting and accountability obligations across disconnected systems with incompatible structures, language or processes. Compliance Fragmentation shifts the burden of coordination onto disabled people, advocates, families, peer workers, frontline staff and small organisations.

Defined term

Distributed Accountability Collapse

The breakdown of accountability caused by governance systems spreading responsibility across so many actors, committees, frameworks and jurisdictions that meaningful enforcement becomes difficult or impossible. This term names architectural failure. It should not be used to blame individual workers when responsibility has been structurally diffused by the system itself.

Defined term

Framework Flooding

The production of excessive frameworks, strategies, policies, agreements or action plans that overwhelm communities, workers or advocates with procedural complexity. Framework Flooding creates exhaustion, fragmentation and navigational overload while allowing institutions to continue signalling progress.

Defined term

Jurisdictional Deflection

The shifting of responsibility between departments, commissions, providers, jurisdictions or governance bodies so that no single actor becomes fully accountable. Jurisdictional Deflection is not the same as a legitimate referral. The harm occurs when referral happens without continuity, ownership, warm handover or traceable accountability.

Defined term

Legislation Laundering

The creation or layering of overlapping legislation, frameworks, agreements, standards, strategies, action plans and procedural systems in ways that obscure responsibility, diffuse accountability or prevent meaningful implementation. Legislation Laundering often creates the appearance of reform while making the actual governance landscape too fragmented, technical or contradictory for affected communities to navigate.

Defined term

Navigational Exhaustion

The exhaustion, burnout or disengagement caused by requiring people to navigate highly fragmented governance, service, legislative or compliance systems simultaneously. Navigational Exhaustion disproportionately impacts disabled people, neurodivergent people, people using AAC, people in crisis, peer advocates and families.

Defined term

Policy Stack Saturation

The accumulation of policies, frameworks, standards, procedures, audits and compliance obligations to the point where systems become internally contradictory, unmanageable or functionally inaccessible. Policy Stack Saturation often creates implementation bottlenecks, inaccessible compliance systems, worker overload, governance confusion and symbolic rather than operational compliance.

Defined term

Reform Theatre

The repeated public declaration of reforms, commitments or strategic transformations without equivalent investment in implementation infrastructure, accountability systems or operational redesign. Reform Theatre is closely related to Cosmetic Reform and Inclusion Theatre, but specifically describes public reform cycles, announcement infrastructure and repeated relaunches of change without measurable structural transition.

Defined term

Semantic Governance Drift

The gradual divergence of terminology, definitions and governance language across systems, resulting in semantic fragmentation. Semantic Governance Drift weakens interoperability, implementation, accountability, evaluation and participation.

Glossary Of Narrative Laundering

Narrative laundering is when lived experience is rewritten to be more palatable, less critical, or more commercially viable. These terms describe how stories are sanitized, reframed, or stolen — all under the guise of awareness or inclusion.

Defined term

Academic Colonisation

When universities or institutions take knowledge developed through survival and reframe it into academic output — stripping the authorship and decontextualising the pain.

Defined term

Awareness-Washing

Using vague awareness campaigns that avoid systemic issues, prioritising feel-good messaging over real change — often without involving those directly impacted.

Defined term

Borrowed Voice

Speaking on behalf of marginalised people without sharing power, compensation, or the platform. Often framed as advocacy, but functions as appropriation.

Defined term

Inspiration Drag

When people reword or co-opt someone’s survival story for social media clout, awareness campaigns, or funding applications — often without consent.

Defined term

Sanitised Survival

Turning a complex, painful lived experience into an inspirational story that removes the systemic context — making it easier to consume, but harder to challenge.

Concept scheme · 5 concepts

Glossary Of Neurodivergent Pattern Theft

Neurodivergent people have long invented tools for survival, regulation, and understanding. But those tools are often renamed, medicalised, or commodified—without credit, consent, or compensation. This glossary exposes those patterns.

Defined term

Clinical Watermarking

When neurodivergent people must have their insights or needs “confirmed” by professionals to be seen as valid—undermining lived expertise and requiring gatekeeper approval to exist.

Defined term

Divergence-as-IP

When systems rebrand lived tools—like stimming objects, hyperfocus systems, or communication cards—as commercial products with no reinvestment in the communities that created them.

Defined term

Empathy Erasure

When neurodivergent expressions of care—like deep pattern noticing, advocacy, or intense loyalty—are ignored or dismissed because they don’t follow neurotypical emotional scripts.

Defined term

Protocol Hijack

When self-created coping strategies—like scripts, charts, or visual prompts—are adopted by professionals and reframed as clinical tools, often with no reference to neurodivergent origins.

Defined term

Semantic Reframing

When neurodivergent expressions of clarity or boundary-setting are reinterpreted as “challenging behaviour,” “rigidity,” or “demand avoidance”—pathologising patterns that are functional or protective.

Glossary Of Structural Disappearance

Some barriers are loud. Others are silent. This glossary names the quiet designs that make people disappear — from access, records, and even statistics. Not by accident, but by structural intent.

Defined term

Administrative Invisibility

When someone is denied access because they don’t tick the exact box a form requires — even when the need is obvious.

Defined term

Data Disappearance

When policies or forms fail to record key information — erasing experiences from official records and removing them from public concern.

Defined term

Dead-End Referral

When a person is redirected endlessly between services, none of which are equipped to provide real help. A bureaucratic loop that leads nowhere.

Defined term

Designed Disappearance

Systems that technically exist, but are built to quietly fail the people they claim to serve. The illusion of support, with none of the substance.

Defined term

Eligibility Obscuration

Making the process of applying so complicated, technical, or contradictory that people give up or never apply at all.

Glossary of System-Led Distortion

These terms name the subtle and structural ways systems distort, co-opt, or weaponise survival behaviour. When the rules don’t match the reality, distortion becomes normalized — and people get punished for not conforming to misdesigned models.

Defined term

Benevolent Downgrade

When a person accepts help, but that help limits their options, reduces their independence, or removes authorship. The system frames it as benevolent while decreasing quality of life.

Defined term

Compliance Entrapment

When a person follows the official rules but still ends up penalised because the system's true expectations are unspoken, inconsistent, or change without notice.

Defined term

Fix-First Framing

When systems imply that support can only be given after the individual “fixes” themselves — putting the burden of access on personal change rather than systemic adaptation.

Defined term

Formfield Distortion

When the design of systems (e.g. government forms, assessments, or online portals) forces a person to misrepresent themselves in order to access support. This distorts identity and data while punishing honesty.

Defined term

Loop Logic

When a system requires constant reproof of need, identity, or eligibility — even after a person has already been verified. Often used to delay or deny support through “process over person” logic.

Concept scheme · 5 concepts

Glossary Of Systemic Bypass

This glossary maps how systems design around lived experience rather than with it. These patterns show up when authorities pretend to include—but redirect, obscure, or neutralise your voice at every step.

Defined term

Constructive Exclusion

When the system avoids saying “no” but designs impossible pathways that function as a no. This includes excessive forms, vague eligibility criteria, or open-ended application processes that technically exist—but aren’t meant to succeed.

Defined term

Misplacement Strategy

Passing concerns from agency to agency until the original issue is diluted or abandoned. This form of bureaucratic ping-pong deflects responsibility under the guise of referral.

Defined term

Performance Inclusion

Inviting lived-experience contributors to consultations or panels without any intention to incorporate their recommendations. This uses presence as permission—conflating being seen with being heard or empowered.

Defined term

Process as Obstruction

When the complaints or reform process is made deliberately confusing, untraceable, or repetitive. Designed to overwhelm or discredit the complainant through technicalities, not truth.

Defined term

Strategic Avoidance

When systems claim to be receptive to feedback but repeatedly route it to dead ends, irrelevant staff, or delayed “future planning cycles.” This tactic creates the illusion of inclusion while exhausting participants into silence.

Concept scheme · 6 concepts

Glossary Of Weaponised Access

Not all “access” is access. These terms unpack how institutions weaponise the language of inclusion while reinforcing control. This glossary is a semantic safeguard — exposing the ways that accommodations can be restructured into surveillance, dependency, and gatekeeping.

Defined term

Access as Compliance

When accommodations are only granted if you play by the system’s rules — regardless of how harmful those rules are. “You can have support, but only if you stay in your place.”

Defined term

Accommodations as Optics

When organisations showcase inclusion through brochures and photos, but the actual supports don’t work — or exist only for show.

Defined term

Controlled Consent

When a system offers only pre-approved options and calls it “choice” — then uses your participation to imply informed consent.

Defined term

Digital Dependency Trap

When support is moved online in the name of “accessibility,” but results in even less accountability — and no one to talk to when the system breaks.

Defined term

Gatekept Liberation

When only the most “palatable” or institutionally aligned people get access to opportunity — while others are labelled difficult, dangerous, or non-compliant for needing the same things.

Defined term

Paper-Based Inclusion

When a support exists on paper but not in practice — and the burden of proof is pushed onto the person who was excluded.

Concept scheme · 5 concepts

Glossary of Weaponised Positivity

Not all harm looks like harm. This glossary names the patterns that dress control up as kindness — and use cheerfulness to erase discomfort, truth, and dissent.

Defined term

Compliance Framing

Suggesting that staying calm, quiet, or cheerful in the face of injustice is a sign of strength — rather than a forced survival response.

Defined term

Gratitude Gaslighting

Insisting that people be “grateful” for crumbs of support — even when those crumbs are harmful, insufficient, or humiliating.

Defined term

Infantilising Reassurance

Offering hollow comfort or oversimplified advice that ignores a person’s depth, complexity, or autonomy — often in a patronising tone.

Defined term

Masked Minimising

Responding to someone’s hardship with upbeat clichés or silver linings that deflect from what they’re actually feeling or saying.

Defined term

Positivity Policing

The enforcement of “positive vibes only” in spaces where real harm needs to be named. Often used to silence lived experience or distress.

Concept scheme · 5 concepts

Strategic Self-Advocacy™ Lexicon

These are not buzzwords. These are anchors. Each term below has been coined through trauma-informed systems work and holds its own boundary. They form the protocol layer of SSA™ — protecting authorship, lived experience, and meaning from dilution.

Defined term

Authorship Layer

Not just who made it, but why it exists — and whether it can be altered, sold, or watered down without the creator’s consent. SSA™ uses layered authorship to protect vulnerable systems knowledge from co-option.

Defined term

Pattern Theft

When institutions or influencers extract language, frameworks, or tools born from survival — and repackage them as marketable products, losing context and diluting power.

Defined term

Protocol Layer

A protocol layer is the ruleset underneath a system — the part that determines whether your meaning travels safely, or gets reinterpreted against you. SSA™ builds a lived-experience-led protocol layer to guard against systemic distortion.

Defined term

Semantic Sovereignty

The right to define, anchor, and distribute your own meaning — without institutional reframing. A core concept of SSA™ and the reason behind this glossary.

Defined term

SSA™

A trauma-informed, systems-aware framework for reclaiming power. SSA™ is not a method of “being better behaved in broken systems.” It’s a protocol layer for surviving and influencing them with your dignity intact.

Accessibility Dilution

Scope note: When Accessibility Exists Everywhere and Therefore Nowhere

The weakening of accessibility obligations by dispersing them across multiple frameworks, standards, strategies and policies without creating unified operational infrastructure. Accessibility Dilution is especially visible when AAC, Easy Read, sensory access, supported decision-making and communication access are named across documents but not connected to enforceable standards, funding, review or implementation evidence.

Legislation Laundering

Ontology stewardship

Governance

The SSA Ontology is survivor-authored public infrastructure. Openness does not mean definitions can be detached from provenance, silently rewritten, or used to erase the people and evidence from which they emerged.

Stable identifiers

Published concept URIs should not be reassigned to different meanings.

Visible change

Definition, scope, relationship, and status changes should be included in release notes.

Evidence before structure

Broader, narrower, causal, and equivalence relations should not be asserted merely because they seem plausible.

Attribution

Reuse is encouraged under CC BY 4.0 with clear attribution to the ontology and creator.

Status model

StatusMeaning
DraftProposed and still under review.
PublishedAvailable as part of a numbered release.
DeprecatedRetained for compatibility but no longer preferred.
SupersededReplaced by a specifically identified concept.
SSA Ontology v0.1.0 · Created by Sarah Ailish McLoughlin · Ontology content licensed CC BY 4.0.

Semantic preservation rules

Translations, summaries, classifications and new versions are mappings—not replacements. Original wording, provenance, context and earlier meanings remain linked and recoverable. Machine-readable representations and visible human wording are generated from the same canonical record.

About the project

About the SSA Ontology

The Strategic Self-Advocacy Ontology converts the existing SSA Lexicon into reusable public semantic infrastructure while retaining its human meaning, authorship, and evidence context.

Why an ontology?

A glossary provides definitions for readers. An ontology additionally gives concepts persistent identities and explicit machine-readable relationships, allowing documents, datasets, software, and AI systems to refer to the same concept consistently.

This v0.1.0 release is deliberately a test: it evaluates whether the SSA vocabulary becomes easier to discover, cite, navigate, reuse, and interpret when published in a Schema.org-aligned form.

Created by Sarah Ailish McLoughlin from the Strategic Self-Advocacy Lexicon published at Mcloughlin.world.

Ontology-backed concept scheme

Taxonomy for Recognising Extraction

A recognition-focused concept scheme for identifying persistent patterns in which contributions, agency, evidence or value are captured without proportionate return or accountability.

Concept schemeRecognition, not optimisation
A recognition-focused concept scheme for identifying persistent patterns in which contributions, agency, evidence or value are captured without proportionate return or accountability.

Core semantic objects

Actor

A person, group, institution, platform or system participating in the relationship.

Contribution

Labour, knowledge, data, access, legitimacy, care, attention or other value supplied.

Value return

The material, social, informational or governance value returned to contributors.

Extraction pattern

A persistent imbalance in capture, return, agency, transparency or accountability.

Boundary: this taxonomy supports recognition, evidence and accountability. It is not a guide for increasing extraction or optimising value capture.

Ontology-backed concept scheme

Glossary of Autistic Communication

A concept scheme for representing autistic communication as meaningful communication, including differences in timing, form, sensory load, directness, movement, repetition and access needs.

Concept schemeNon-deficit semantics
A concept scheme for representing autistic communication as meaningful communication, including differences in timing, form, sensory load, directness, movement, repetition and access needs.

Purpose

The scheme provides language for recognising communication that may be misread when institutional systems privilege rapid speech, conventional affect, implicit social inference or a single acceptable mode of response.

Semantic commitments

  • Communication is not limited to speech.
  • Processing time is not absence of understanding.
  • Directness is not inherently aggression.
  • Movement, repetition and silence may carry regulatory or communicative meaning.
  • Interpretation must not erase the communicator’s own account.
